definition: A divine power or presence, often attached to a place, object or action rather than to a fully anthropomorphic god. Roman religion used the idea to describe the force behind natural and social life.
A Roman virtue meaning dutiful conduct toward the gods, one's family, and the community. It is not simply piety in the modern sense, but a whole set of obligations.
Household gods who protected the family and its storeroom. The Roman state also had public Penates, and Aeneas was said to have carried them from Troy.
Guardian spirits of the household, crossroads and neighbourhood. Families honoured the Lares at the hearth and at small shrines within the home.
The reading of signs, especially the flight and feeding of birds, to learn whether the gods approved an action. Roman magistrates relied on augurs before public business.
Priestesses of Vesta who tended the sacred hearth of Rome and were bound by strict vows of chastity. Their service was central to the state cult.
The 'peace of the gods', the proper relationship between the Roman state and its deities. It was maintained through sacrifice, festival and careful ritual.
Virgil's epic poem, composed under Augustus, telling of Aeneas' journey from Troy to Italy and the founding of the Roman line.
Ovid's long poem of transformation myths, written in the early empire. It retells Greek and Roman stories and was enormously influential in later European art.
The two-faced god of beginnings, doorways and transitions. The doors of his temple in Rome were closed in peacetime and open in war.
